canonical_statement: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases inactivate most penicillins, cephalosporins, and aztreonam.
ESBL-producing Enterobacterales generally remain susceptible to carbapenems.
ESBL enzymes do not inactivate non-beta-lactam agents, but ESBL-carrying organisms often harbor additional resistance determinants that broaden resistance.
ESBL genes can occur in gram-negative organisms but are most prevalent in Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Klebsiella oxytoca.
CTX-M enzymes, particularly CTX-M-15, are the most common ESBLs in the United States.
Routine ESBL testing is not performed by most clinical microbiology laboratories and is not compulsory under CLSI guidance.
For E. coli, K. pneumoniae, and K. oxytoca, ceftriaxone resistance with MIC at least 4 micrograms/mL is commonly used as a surrogate threshold for ESBL production.
The ESBL-E treatment suggestions in this section assume in vitro susceptibility to the preferred or alternative antibiotic has been demonstrated.
For ESBL-E uncomplicated UTI, the panel lists single-dose aminoglycosides, gepotidacin, nitrofurantoin, pivmecillinam, sulopenem, and TMP-SMX as preferred options without preferential ordering.
Single-dose oral fosfomycin is an alternative option for uncomplicated UTI caused by ESBL-producing E. coli.
When resistance, availability, or intolerance precludes preferred or alternative uncomplicated-UTI agents, fluoroquinolones, cefepime-enmetazobactam, or carbapenems may be used.
ESBL-producing E. coli accounts for approximately 17% of UTIs in the United States, with substantial regional variability.
Surveillance data indicate susceptibility above 90% for several preferred and alternative agents used for ESBL-E uncomplicated UTI.
A systematic review of 13 studies including 13,804 patients reported approximately 95% pooled microbiologic cure after single-dose aminoglycoside therapy.

population.label: Patients treated with single-dose aminoglycoside therapy

canonical_statement: In the same systematic review, 73% of patients had no recurrence by day 30 after single-dose aminoglycoside therapy.

population.label: Patients treated with single-dose aminoglycoside therapy

canonical_statement: The panel considers single-dose aminoglycoside therapy a preferred approach for ESBL-E uncomplicated UTI despite limited robust clinical-trial data.
Gepotidacin demonstrates in vitro activity against more than 90% of ESBL-E isolates.
In one randomized trial subgroup of women with ESBL-producing E. coli uncomplicated UTI, treatment success was 70% with gepotidacin and 63% with nitrofurantoin.

population.label: Women with ESBL-producing E. coli uUTI

canonical_statement: In a second randomized trial subgroup of women with ESBL-producing E. coli uncomplicated UTI, treatment success was 68% with gepotidacin and 40% with nitrofurantoin.

population.label: Women with ESBL-producing E. coli uUTI

canonical_statement: Mild to moderate diarrhea is the most common adverse event reported with gepotidacin.
Because gepotidacin is active against Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the panel cautions that excessive use could select resistant N. gonorrhoeae strains.
Nitrofurantoin susceptibility among ESBL-E generally exceeds 90%.
In a randomized trial of E. coli uncomplicated UTI, treatment success was 70% with 5-day nitrofurantoin and 58% with single-dose oral fosfomycin.
The nitrofurantoin-versus-fosfomycin randomized trial did not specify ESBL status, so applicability to ESBL-E uncomplicated UTI is extrapolated rather than directly demonstrated.
Pivmecillinam demonstrates in vitro activity against more than 90% of ESBL-E isolates.
Three-day pivmecillinam regimens achieve treatment success in approximately 75% to 95% of women with uncomplicated UTI.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: reported range midpoint not calculated; lower bound represented

canonical_statement: Observational data suggest increased failure with pivmecillinam for ESBL-E versus non-ESBL-E uncomplicated UTI, but this difference was not observed with 400 mg three times daily.
Sulopenem is active in vitro against more than 95% of ESBL-E isolates.
For ESBL-E uncomplicated UTI, 5 days of sulopenem had treatment success of 56% versus 47% with a 3-day ciprofloxacin course.
Probenecid in the sulopenem etzadroxil-probenecid formulation inhibits tubular secretion and may increase plasma concentrations of drugs such as methotrexate, piperacillin, and sulfonamides.
United States surveillance suggests only about 50% of ESBL-E urinary isolates are susceptible to TMP-SMX.
TMP-SMX is effective as a three-day course for ESBL-E uncomplicated UTI when the isolate is susceptible, but empiric use requires close monitoring because susceptibility is limited.
Oral fosfomycin is not suggested for gram-negative uncomplicated UTI organisms other than E. coli because organisms such as K. pneumoniae commonly harbor fosA genes that may inactivate fosfomycin.
Clinical outcome studies directly evaluating the impact of fosA on fosfomycin efficacy are not available.
The clinical benefit of multidose oral fosfomycin for uncomplicated UTI remains uncertain.
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is not suggested for ESBL-E uncomplicated UTI.
In a randomized trial of 370 women with E. coli uncomplicated UTI, clinical cure was 58% with three-day amoxicillin-clavulanate and 77% with three-day ciprofloxacin.
In the same trial, persistent vaginal bacterial colonization occurred in 45% with amoxicillin-clavulanate versus 10% with ciprofloxacin.
The proportion of participants with ESBL-E isolates in the amoxicillin-clavulanate versus ciprofloxacin trial was not reported, and both regimens used lower doses than suggested in the guidance.
Only 35% to 60% of doxycycline is excreted unchanged in urine.
The panel suggests avoiding doxycycline for ESBL-E uncomplicated UTI because of relatively low urinary concentrations and limited interpretable clinical data.

The panel suggests reserving cefepime-enmetazobactam, susceptible fluoroquinolones, and carbapenems for cUTI or invasive ESBL-E infections rather than uncomplicated UTI when effective narrower alternatives are available.
For ESBL-E complicated UTI, TMP-SMX, ciprofloxacin, or levofloxacin are preferred when in vitro susceptibility is demonstrated.
Cefepime-enmetazobactam or carbapenems are preferred for ESBL-E complicated UTI when resistance, intolerance, or toxicity precludes TMP-SMX or fluoroquinolones.
IV fosfomycin, aminoglycosides, and piperacillin-tazobactam are alternative options for ESBL-E complicated UTI.
When IV therapy has been started for ESBL-E complicated UTI, transition to oral TMP-SMX, ciprofloxacin, or levofloxacin is preferred once susceptibility is demonstrated.
In a randomized cUTI trial subgroup with ESBL-E, treatment success was 74% with cefepime-enmetazobactam and 52% with piperacillin-tazobactam.
Direct comparisons of cefepime-enmetazobactam with carbapenems for ESBL-E complicated UTI are lacking.
Among 111 patients with ESBL-E complicated UTI, 7 days of IV fosfomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam each produced 93% clinical cure.
In an open-label trial of 81 patients with presumed ESBL E. coli cUTI and bacteremia, clinical and microbiological cure was 59% with IV fosfomycin and 71% with meropenem.

population.label: Patients with presumed ESBL E. coli cUTI and bacteremia

canonical_statement: IV fosfomycin did not achieve noninferiority to comparator agents in the overall trial, and additional data are needed before it can be considered preferred therapy.

source_anchor.paragraph: Question 1.2 rationale - IV fosfomycin evidence limitation

canonical_statement: The sodium content of IV fosfomycin warrants caution in older adults and patients at risk for heart failure.
In a K. pneumoniae cUTI subgroup, clinical cure was 93% with 7-day IV fosfomycin and 100% with piperacillin-tazobactam.
The panel advises careful consideration before using IV fosfomycin for ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae because fosA is frequently present and may inactivate fosfomycin.
Aminoglycosides are alternative options for ESBL-E complicated UTI, but duration-dependent nephrotoxicity should be considered.
In a randomized trial of cUTI, clinical cure was 89% with plazomicin and 90% with meropenem.
In the same cUTI trial, acute kidney injury occurred in 7% of plazomicin recipients and 4% of meropenem recipients.
Among patients with ESBL-E cUTI in the plazomicin trial, microbiological eradication was 82% with plazomicin and 75% with meropenem.
Aminoglycosides may be reasonable for terminal doses when completing cUTI treatment because of prolonged renal cortical activity and once-daily dosing convenience.
In a randomized cUTI trial, sulopenem did not meet noninferiority for the day-21 combined clinical and microbiologic response: 68% versus 74% with ertapenem-based therapy.

exposures.details: 5 initial days IV sulopenem then oral therapy
5 initial days IV ertapenem then oral therapy

concept.text: Combined clinical and microbiologic response at day 21

canonical_statement: In the sulopenem cUTI trial, overall clinical success was 89% with sulopenem and 88% with ertapenem-based therapy.
Among patients with ESBL-positive infection in the sulopenem cUTI trial, favorable response was 72% with sulopenem and 68% with ertapenem-based therapy.
Oral sulopenem is suggested only as an alternative for ESBL-E cUTI after initial clinical improvement, because the supporting trial included five initial days of IV therapy.

Oral fosfomycin is not suggested as initial therapy for cUTI because renal parenchymal concentrations are limited, but it may be considered for transition therapy in selected ESBL E. coli cUTI when other oral options are unavailable.
Trials of multidose oral fosfomycin after IV therapy included limited ESBL-E representation, and IV lead-in durations often approximated the full usual cUTI treatment duration.

canonical_statement: Ertapenem, imipenem, and meropenem are preferred for ESBL-E infections outside the urinary tract.
Imipenem or meropenem are preferred over ertapenem for critically ill patients or patients with hypoalbuminemia.
Cefepime-enmetazobactam is an alternative option for ESBL-E infections outside the urinary tract.
After an appropriate clinical response, oral ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, or TMP-SMX may be used as transition therapy for non-urinary ESBL-E infection when susceptibility is demonstrated.
In an open-label trial of ESBL-E bloodstream infection, 30-day survival was 88% with piperacillin-tazobactam and 96% with meropenem.
In a reanalysis restricted to isolates with piperacillin-tazobactam MIC at most 16 micrograms/mL by broth microdilution, 30-day survival was 91% with piperacillin-tazobactam and 96% with meropenem.
In the bloodstream-infection reanalysis, the absolute risk-difference confidence interval was -1% to 11% and was no longer statistically significant.
Despite attenuation in the reanalysis, the panel continues to favor carbapenems for ESBL-producing bloodstream infection because the mortality direction was consistent overall and across subgroups.
The panel extrapolates bloodstream-infection evidence to other common ESBL-E sites including intra-abdominal infection, skin and soft tissue infection, and pneumonia.
Hypoalbuminemia increases the unbound fraction of highly protein-bound ertapenem, increasing clearance and shortening serum half-life.
An observational study of 279 patients with Enterobacterales infection associated albumin below 2.5 g/dL with higher odds of 30-day mortality for ertapenem versus imipenem or meropenem.
Clinical data comparing ertapenem with other carbapenems in critically ill patients are limited and conflicting.
Evidence that higher-dose or more frequent ertapenem improves outcomes in obesity, critical illness, or hypoalbuminemia is limited.
PK/PD modeling supports adequate intrapulmonary penetration and high target attainment for cefepime-enmetazobactam against Enterobacterales with MICs at most 8/8 micrograms/mL.
Clinical data for cefepime-enmetazobactam in ESBL-E infections outside the urinary tract remain limited, preventing its designation as preferred therapy.
Oral TMP-SMX or fluoroquinolone step-down for ESBL-E infection should require confirmed susceptibility, hemodynamic stability, and no concern for impaired gastrointestinal absorption.

Nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, omadacycline, and doxycycline are not suggested as oral step-down therapy for ESBL-E bloodstream infection because of serum-exposure concerns and/or limited supporting data.

canonical_statement: Oral sulopenem is not suggested as transition therapy for ESBL-E bloodstream infection pending additional PK/PD and clinical data.
In a cUTI-bacteremia subgroup, treatment success was 57% after transition to oral sulopenem versus 65% after transition to oral ciprofloxacin or amoxicillin-clavulanate.

population.label: Patients with cUTI and associated bacteremia

concept.text: Oral ciprofloxacin or amoxicillin-clavulanate after IV ertapenem

canonical_statement: In a randomized intra-abdominal infection trial, clinical success was 82% with a sulopenem strategy and 88% with an ertapenem-based comparator strategy.

exposures.details: 5 days IV sulopenem then oral sulopenem
5 days IV ertapenem then oral ciprofloxacin/metronidazole or amoxicillin-clavulanate

canonical_statement: If empiric piperacillin-tazobactam was started for ESBL-E uncomplicated UTI and the patient improves clinically, neither changing therapy nor extending treatment duration is necessary.
Piperacillin-tazobactam is an alternative for ESBL-E complicated UTI only in patients who are not critically ill and do not have concomitant bacteremia.
Piperacillin-tazobactam is not suggested for ESBL-E infections outside the urinary tract even when in vitro susceptibility is demonstrated.
Piperacillin-tazobactam MIC testing may be inaccurate or poorly reproducible in the presence of ESBLs or other beta-lactamases such as OXA-1.
Preclinical data indicate greater regrowth of ESBL-E with piperacillin-tazobactam than meropenem at increased bacterial inoculum, although the clinical implications are uncertain.
Tazobactam effectiveness may be reduced when ESBL expression is increased or multiple ESBL or AmpC enzymes are present.
Piperacillin-tazobactam contains an 8:1 piperacillin-to-tazobactam ratio, whereas ceftolozane-tazobactam contains a 2:1 beta-lactam-to-tazobactam ratio.
A systematic review of one randomized trial and six observational studies comprising 1,156 patients found comparable treatment success with piperacillin-tazobactam and carbapenems for ESBL-E UTIs.
In a 66-patient ESBL-E cUTI trial, treatment success was 94% with piperacillin-tazobactam and 97% with ertapenem.
In the urinary-source bloodstream-infection subgroup, survival was 93% with piperacillin-tazobactam and 97% with meropenem.

population.label: Patients with ESBL-E bloodstream infection from a urinary source

canonical_statement: The panel does not suggest piperacillin-tazobactam for ESBL-E cUTI in critically ill patients or when bacteremia is present.
A 2023 meta-analysis of 2,786 patients found no survival difference between beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor regimens and carbapenems for ESBL-E bloodstream infection.
One subsequent observational study reported 92% survival with piperacillin-tazobactam and 92% with carbapenem therapy.

population.label: Patients with ESBL-E infection in observational study

canonical_statement: Another observational study reported 86% survival with empiric piperacillin-tazobactam and 96% with comparator therapy.

population.label: Patients with ESBL-E infection in observational study

canonical_statement: Given preclinical inoculum concerns and clinical-trial signals of worse outcomes, piperacillin-tazobactam is not suggested as preferred or alternative therapy for invasive ESBL-E infection.
If empiric cefepime was started for ESBL-E uncomplicated UTI and the patient improves clinically, changing therapy or extending the duration is unnecessary.
The panel suggests avoiding cefepime for ESBL-E complicated UTI and for infections outside the urinary tract even when cefepime susceptibility is demonstrated.
ESBL enzymes commonly hydrolyze cefepime when it is not protected by a beta-lactamase inhibitor.
Commercial cefepime MIC testing can be inaccurate or poorly reproducible for ESBL-producing isolates.
Clinical trials directly comparing cefepime with carbapenems for ESBL-E bloodstream infection have not been conducted.
In an ESBL-E cUTI trial, clinical success was 33% with cefepime and 97% with ertapenem, and the cefepime arm was terminated early for a clinical-failure signal.
In a pneumonia subgroup with ESBL-E, clinical success was 69% with cefepime and 100% with imipenem.
The panel suggests avoiding cefepime for invasive ESBL-E infections.
Cephamycins are not suggested for ESBL-E infection until additional clinical outcomes data with cefoxitin or cefotetan and optimized dosing are available.
Cephamycins are generally stable against hydrolysis by ESBL enzymes.
Cefoxitin and cefotetan are the only cephamycins available in the United States, and both are IV formulations.
Across at least 10 observational comparisons of cephamycins versus carbapenems for ESBL-E infection, eight reported no outcome difference and two reported poorer outcomes with cephamycins.
The largest cited cephamycin study reported 30-day survival of 71% with cephamycins versus 87% with carbapenems among patients with ESBL-E bacteremia.
Cephamycin comparative evidence is limited by observational design, heterogeneous infection sources, selection bias, and variable agents, dosing strategies, and treatment durations.
The most encouraging cephamycin data are for cefmetazole, which is not available for clinical use in the United States.
Relatively few patients in clinical investigations have received cefoxitin or cefotetan, and additional optimized dosing and administration data are needed.
Even though limited data suggest potential benefit from high-dose continuous-infusion cefoxitin, its IV-only formulation and short half-life offer no clear advantage over preferred ESBL-E agents.

Although active against ESBL-E, aztreonam-avibactam, ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-relebactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, and cefiderocol should preferentially be reserved for carbapenem-resistant organisms.
Aztreonam-avibactam, ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-relebactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, and cefiderocol exhibit activity against ESBL-E.
Avibactam can protect aztreonam and ceftazidime from hydrolysis by ESBL enzymes.
Clinical-trial subgroup analyses support ceftazidime-avibactam effectiveness against ESBL-E infection.
The carbapenem components of meropenem-vaborbactam and imipenem-relebactam provide sufficient activity against ESBL-E even without their beta-lactamase inhibitors.
Ceftolozane-tazobactam is more potent against ESBL-E than piperacillin-tazobactam and is more stable to hydrolysis by common ESBL enzymes such as CTX-M-15.
The ceftolozane-to-tazobactam ratio is 2:1 compared with an 8:1 piperacillin-to-tazobactam ratio, resulting in greater relative tazobactam concentration with ceftolozane-tazobactam.
In randomized-trial subgroups with ESBL-E intra-abdominal infection or UTI, clinical cure was 97% with ceftolozane-tazobactam and 89% with meropenem.

population.label: Patients with ESBL-E intra-abdominal infection or UTI

canonical_statement: In an ESBL-E pneumonia trial subgroup, 28-day survival was 79% with ceftolozane-tazobactam and 71% with meropenem.
The panel reserves these broad beta-lactam agents for carbapenem-resistant organisms or polymicrobial infection involving organisms that exhibit carbapenem resistance.
